is a text-based way to interact with your computer:
Search for “Command Prompt” or “PowerShell” in Start menu

# See where you are
cd

# List files in current directory
dir

# Go to your Documents folder
cd Documents

# Create a new folder
mkdir ProgrammingClass

# Enter the new folder
cd ProgrammingClass

# Go back to parent directory
cd ..

# Start a program
notepad.exe

# See where you are
pwd

# List files in current directory
ls

# Go to your Documents folder
cd Documents

# Create a new folder
mkdir ProgrammingClass

# Enter the new folder
cd ProgrammingClass

# Go back to parent directory
cd ..

# Start a program
open -a TextEdit
is a running program in memory:
: Each process has its own memory space
: Waiting to be assigned to the CPU
: Waiting for some event (I/O, signals, etc.)
: Execution completed, but still in memory
: Process created but not yet admitted to the pool of executable processes
Graphical interface to view and manage running processes
Monitor CPU, memory, disk, and network usage

# List all running processes
tasklist

# Find specific processes by name
tasklist | findstr "notepad"

# Kill a process by name (force with /F)
taskkill /IM notepad.exe
taskkill /F /IM notepad.exe

# Kill a process by PID (force with /F)
taskkill /PID 1234
taskkill /F /PID 1234

# Start a program
start notepad.exe
GUI tool for monitoring and managing processes
Shows CPU, memory, energy, disk, and network usage

# List running processes
ps aux

# Find specific process
ps aux | grep "TextEdit"

# Kill a process by PID
kill 1234

# Force kill a process (SIGKILL)
kill -9 1234

# Kill process by name
killall TextEdit

# Start a program
open -a TextEdit

# View process hierarchy
pstree

# View all environment variables
set # gci env: in PowerShell

# View specific variable

echo %USERPROFILE%

# Set a variable (temporary)

env

# View specific variable

echo $HOME

# Set a variable (temporary)

Directories where executable files are found

: The PATH environment variable is crucial for program accessibility. When software is installed, it must add its directory to PATH; otherwise you can only run the program by typing its absolute path. This is why properly installed programs can be launched from any location in the terminal by simply typing their name.

Why VMs or Containers when we already have apps?

children.label: Why VMs or Containers when we already have apps?

children.value: : Applications run in their own environment without interfering with the host system
: Some applications may not be compatible with the user’s operating system
: Applications may have complex dependencies that conflict with other installed software
: VMs or containers provide a self-contained “package” that can be executed consistently across different environments
: Ensures consistent behavior regardless of where the application runs
: Containment of potential security vulnerabilities within the VM/container boundary
: Better control over CPU, memory, and storage allocation
: Easier to scale applications horizontally by deploying multiple instances

Containers are primarily used for deploying non-graphical applications (although Flatpak and Snap on Linux are an exception). They have become the industry standard for deploying services in cloud environments, especially web services, due to their lightweight nature and efficient resource utilization.

: For users, containers typically means using Docker. Docker runs Linux-based applications, so on macOS and Windows, it requires a lightweight Linux-based VM. On Linux, Docker can run natively without an additional VM layer.
